newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia Airline year profits seen lacklustre- analysts.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia Airline year profits seen lacklustre- analysts.

text.p: Profits at national carrier Malaysia Airline System Bhd (MAS) are expected to be higher for the year ended March 31, 1997, but not enough to excite investors, analysts said.
The company is expected to release its full-year results on Thursday.

The Estimate Directory, which polled 31 analysts covering Malaysia Airlines, projects net profit to be 261 million ringgit ($103.74 million). MAS reported net profit of 233 million ringgit in the previous comparable year.
Despite the expected profit rise, concerns over the company's high debt levels, fuel costs amd competition, are keeping recommendations firmly neutral, analysts said.

"I'm quite pessimistic. Last month it (the share price) had fallen to around 5.35 ringgit, when I raised my recommendation to a 'hold' from a 'sell'," said an airlines analyst at a foreign equities research house in Kuala Lumpur.
MAS shares closed at 5.65 ringgit on Tuesday.

"There are a lot of uncertainties. They have had a huge amount of capex (capital expenditure) in the course of buying new aircraft and in their move to Sepang (the new Kuala Lumpur International Airport which is due for completion in 1998)," the analyst added.
The airline is also going to face competition from smaller local airlines like Air Asia and Saeaga with which it has to share landing rights, said the analyst.

Even though MAS's fund-raising exercises earlier in the year were designed to redice its gearing, its debts are expected to remain at a multiple of between one and 1.5-times shareholders' funds, said analysts.

In May 1996, the airline had announced a private placement of 17 million shares at eight ringgit each. This was followed by a one-for-one rights issue priced at 2.30 ringgit and a 1.5 billion ringgit bond issue earlier this year.
This week, MAS said it had signed agreements with a consortium of financial institutions to raise 50 billion yen in debt through Euroyen and floating rate note issues.

"This year the rights and bond issues will take care of the financing concerns. The concerns are now more on the service standards and the operating costs," said Choo Swee Kee, airlines analyst at Vickers Ballas in Kuala Lumpur.
MAS was criticised by local consumer groups late in 1996 for declining service quality on its flights. The airline said it had taken steps to fix the problems.

The signing of an "open skies" pact with the United States earlier this year was seen by analysts as potentially beneficial to profits in the coming years, as it would allow MAS to fly to more cities within the U.S.

Falling jet fuel prices in 1997 would also help the airline's bottom line, they said. Fuel prices jumped 13 percent in the first nine months of 1996, and fuel costs make up about 15 percent of MAS's total expenses.

"Oil prices have been very volatile. Prices have come back down this year," said Declan Magee, regional airlines analyst at ABN Amro Hoare Govett in Hong Kong. "But this would not have been reflected in the earnings as yet," he added.
Passenger volumes have increased, but "the actual price per ticket has come under a lot of pressure," said Magee.
He said this was a result of increased competition from other regional carriers such as Hong Kong's Cathay Pacific and Singapore Airlines
